title: Psalm 46: God Is Our Refuge and Strength
summary: The psalm declares that God is his people's refuge and strength, so they will not fear even if the earth gives way and the mountains fall into the sea. A river gladdens the city of God, and God is within her, so she will not be moved while nations rage. The psalm ends with God's own voice: “Be still and know that I am God”, and a refrain that the LORD of Hosts is with us.
story: Psalm 46 is the first of three songs in a row celebrating God's presence in Zion (Psalms 46, 47, and 48). After the defeat lamented in Psalm 44 and the royal hope of Psalm 45, the Psalter turns to confidence: the city stands not because of its walls or its army but because God dwells in it. The psalm belongs to a small group scholars call the Songs of Zion (usually including 46, 48, 76, 84, 87, and 122). It looks back to God's victories and forward to the day when he will end war across the whole earth.
historical:
The heading assigns the psalm to the sons of Korah and sets it “According to Alamoth”, a musical term found also in 1 Chronicles 15:20. The word resembles the Hebrew for young women, and many think it means a high register, perhaps sopranos or high-pitched instruments, though this is uncertain.

No event is named. Many interpreters have linked the psalm to 701 BC, when the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah, and the city was spared when the Assyrian army withdrew (2 Kings 18 and 19; Isaiah 36 and 37). The phrase “when morning dawns” (verse 5) reminds some readers of that account, where the Assyrian dead are found in the morning (2 Kings 19:35). Others think the psalm was written for worship at the temple, celebrating God's protection of Zion in general terms, and was not tied to a single deliverance. Both views agree that it expresses a confidence rooted in Jerusalem's temple and God's promises to David.
cultural:
Jerusalem has no river. Its water came from the Gihon spring and from cisterns, and Hezekiah cut a tunnel to bring the spring's water inside the walls. The river whose streams delight the city of God is therefore a picture, drawing on the ancient image of a river flowing from the dwelling of God, as in Eden's river (Genesis 2:10) and the river Ezekiel sees flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47). In the ancient Near East the raging sea often symbolized chaos, and the psalm pictures the waters roaring and the mountains shaking, with God's city calm in the middle.

The title “LORD of Hosts” names God as commander of armies, heavenly and earthly. Bows, spears, and shields were the standard weapons of ancient warfare; after a victory, captured weapons were sometimes burned. In verse 9 God does this to the weapons of the whole earth. The psalm's first line inspired Martin Luther's hymn known in English as A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, written in the late 1520s.
literary: Three stanzas are marked off by “Selah” (a term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical direction) and by a refrain in verses 7 and 11. Many scholars think the refrain once also stood after verse 3. The first stanza (verses 1 to 3) is about nature in upheaval; the second (verses 4 to 7) about the city and the nations in turmoil; the third (verses 8 to 11) about God's action ending war. The same verb for shaking or being moved ties them together: the mountains totter, the kingdoms totter, but God's city will not be moved. In verse 10 the speaker changes, and God himself speaks.

outline.t: No fear, though the earth gives way
The river and the city of God
Come and see: God ends war, be still

doctrines.note: The psalm pictures the worst imaginable instability, the earth itself collapsing, and insists God is still present and helping. Providence here is not the absence of trouble but God's reliable presence within it.
Nations rage and kingdoms crumble, but when God lifts his voice the earth melts. He will be exalted among the nations. No human power has the last word.

The vision of God making wars cease to the end of the earth looks forward to a peace no human treaty has achieved, the hope the prophets expressed when they spoke of swords beaten into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4).

words.note: Machaseh, refuge or shelter, a place to flee to when danger comes. It is one of the Psalter's favorite words for God. The psalm opens by naming God himself, not the city or its walls, as the refuge.

Misgav, a high, secure place, a stronghold out of reach (translated fortress in verses 7 and 11). The refrain pairs it with the name “God of Jacob”, the patriarch who was protected despite his weakness.

Raphah, to let go, relax, or stop. Behind “Be still” is a command to drop one's hands and cease striving. In context it is addressed to the raging nations as much as to the faithful: stop fighting, and recognize who is God.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 46, so the connection to Christ is thematic. The psalm's central claim is that God is with his people, which the refrain states twice. Matthew's Gospel opens by calling Jesus Immanuel, which means God with us (Matthew 1:23), and closes with his promise to be with his disciples always (Matthew 28:20). The river that gladdens the city of God reappears in Revelation 22, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the new Jerusalem. The psalm's hope that God will make wars cease belongs to the peace Christ announces and will complete.
questions: The psalm imagines the mountains falling into the sea. What in your life feels like the ground giving way, and what would it mean to call God your refuge there?
“Be still and know that I am God” is often read as a call to quiet devotion. How does reading it as a command to the warring nations change it?
The psalm finds security in God's presence rather than in walls or armies. What walls do you rely on instead?
